name: Nawuri
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Sherwood, Barbara. 1982. A grammatical description of Nawuri. PhD thesis, SOAS, Univ. of London; also Casali, Roderic F. 1995. Nawuri ATR harmony (SAL 24)
earlier_scan.note: Sherwood 1982 SOAS grammar plausibly covers prosody; SOAS eprints DNS-unreachable, SIL 403

new_statements.quote: Nawuri has two contrastive tones, high (H) and low (L). Like many African tonal languages, the language displays the phenomenon of downdrift, in which the second of two H tones separated by an intervening L is pronounced at a slightly lower pitch than the first H. Cases of downstep, in which the second of two H's is pronounced at a lower pitch level even when no L-toned syllable intervenes, are also not uncommon. [...] Contour rising and falling tones also occur in Nawuri; as in most West African tonal languages, these may be analyzed as arising from sequences of level (H and L) tones.
new_statements.citation: Casali, Roderic F. 1994. Nominal tone in Nawuri. Journal of West African Languages 24(2): 45-64.
new_statements.locator: Section 1 'Background', p. 46 (PDF p. 2; scanned file page p-001)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nawuri is described as a two-level tone language (H, L) with downdrift, downstep and derived contours; the accessible descriptions (Casali 1994 tone article; Casali 1995 phonological background sketch, p. 64: 'There are two contrastive tone levels in Nawuri, high and low') say nothing at all about word stress, neither locating it nor denying it.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal details: falling tones almost entirely word-final and realized only pre-pausally; rising contours restricted mostly to bimoraic monosyllabic imperatives; a downstepped-fall contour on some imperfective monosyllabic verbs (Casali 1994: 46-47).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone description (nouns with class prefixes, Kitare dialect, author's own fieldwork). Casali 1995 (p. 64) adds that independent words are minimally CV and that subject pronouns are clitics. No stress domain can be stated because stress is not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened Casali sources describe the Kitare-village dialect (Northern Region, Ghana); Casali 1990 fn 3 notes that Sherwood 1982 describes the Kpandai dialect, which differs 'in certain respects' (segmental contrasts). Both are Nawuri nawu1242; no separate glottocodes for the dialects.

Like many African tonal languages, the language displays the phenomenon of downdrift, in which the second of two H tones separated by an intervening L is pronounced at a slightly lower pitch than the first H. sources.locator: Section 1 'Background', p. 46 (PDF p. 2; scanned file page p-001)
sources.note: Section 1 Background (pp. 46-47): two contrastive tones H and L; downdrift; non-automatic downstep analysed as floating L; rising and falling contours = sequences of level tones; falling tones almost entirely word-final and only pre-pausal; syllable types CV, CVN, CVV; heavy = long vowel or nasal coda. No mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the 20 pages (grep of the full scanned).

sources.citation: Casali, Roderic F. 1990. Contextual labialization in Nawuri. Studies in African Linguistics 21(3): 319-346. doi:10.32473/sal.v21i3.107430
sources.note: Segmental (labialization) study; no occurrence of stress/accent/prominence in the text layer. Fn 1: data are the Kitare dialect (fieldwork Dec 1985-Apr 1988); fn 3: Sherwood 1982 describes the Kpandai dialect, which differs in certain respects; p. 320 refers to Casali 1988 as 'a fuller description of Nawuri phonology'.

sources.citation: Casali, Roderic F. 2002. Nawuri ATR harmony in typological perspective. Journal of West African Languages 29(1): 3-43.
sources.note: Vowel-harmony study; the opening pages read (abstract, introduction, vowel inventory) say nothing about stress; only 'tone-bearing behavior' of vowels is mentioned. Remaining 36 pages not scanned.

sources.citation: Casali, Roderic F. 1996. Resolving hiatus. PhD dissertation, UCLA. Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-215.
sources.note: Cross-linguistic study; Nawuri appears ~30 times (vowel elision, interconsonantal centralization of front vowels, 9-vowel ATR system, postlexical rightward [+ATR] spreading across word boundaries) but there is no statement about Nawuri stress. Useful for its bibliography: Casali 1988 'Vowel clusters and syllable structure in Nawuri' (Papers in Ghanaian Linguistics 7), Casali 1995 'Nawuri Phonology' (Language Monographs 3, Legon), Snider 1989a North Guang comparative word list.

sources.citation: Casali, Roderic F. 1995. An overview of the Nawuri verbal system. Journal of West African Languages 25(1): 63-86.
sources.note: Phonological background (p. 64) gives consonant and vowel inventories, Akan-type [ATR] harmony, roundness harmony, contrastive vowel length, and 'two contrastive tone levels in Nawuri, high and low' with downdrift and downstep; independent words minimally CV, subject pronouns are clitics. Nothing on stress. Fn 2 (p. 63) lists the phonology literature: Casali 1988, 1990, forthcoming a,b; Snider 1989a,b,c, 1990; Sherwood 1982 for syntax and morphology.
